I've been able to mix my awakened and dream states a little, and I can actually answer the question: a lot. When I'm dreaming half or more of my brain/thought time is spent deciding what's realistic. It's not just physics though. A lot of dreaming is brainstorming what has and what might happen. If you almost fall that night you're likely to dream about it several times and that helps you brainstorm out what you might have done differently. If you have a difficult conversation you could brainstorm out what things you might have said differently.

A lot of physics is just what you're used to happening, so there's no need to do physics math any more than you do when you're awake. But if any dreams involve odd motions you will find excuses for why your body isn't moving/tired/breathing hard when you're dreaming of such situations.

Your brain likely cheats in that regard. It's not stimulating physics to an exact degree but rather an analog faux physics based on waking observations. Your brain isn't calculating the mass and velocity of moving objects but rather referencing objects in motion you've witnessed while awake. I feel like animals would likely dream in the same fashion only limited to things they've experienced personally and not so much extravagant works of fiction loosely based on your own experiences.
